newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany seeks Northern Irish republican's daughter.
newsitem.headline: Germany seeks Northern Irish republican's daughter.

text.p: Germany on Monday said it had asked Northern Ireland to extradite the daughter of former Irish republican politician Bernadette McAliskey, nee Devlin, for questioning about an IRA mortar attack last June.
The federal prosecutor's office in Karlsruhe said it wanted to question Roisin McAliskey about the attack which damaged buildings at a British army base near the northwest German town of Osnabrueck.
"I can confirm that an arrest warrant has been issued," a spokesman said. The British Broadcasting Corporation said McAliskey, 25, had been in police custody for six days.
"A woman is currently in custody in Northern Ireland and an extradition warrant has been sworn by the German authorities in London this morning," said a Northern Irish police spokeswoman.

Bernadette Devlin was a leading figure in Northern Irish civil rights marches during the 1960s. She became the youngest woman to be elected to the British parliament when she took her seat on her 22nd birthday in 1969.

A few months later she was sentenced to six months in prison for inciting people to riot and disorderly behaviour after she urged Catholic residents of Londonderry to raise barricades against police during the 1969 "Battle of the Bogside."
In 1972 she again hit the headlines for punching Home Secretary (interior minister) Reginald Maudling in parliament. She lost her parliament seat two years later and now rarely appears in public.
Roisin was with her in 1994 when she attended the funeral of republican guerrilla Dominic McGlinchey.
Bernadette McAliskey made a graveside speech in which she described McGlinchey as "the finest republican the struggle has ever produced."
The attack at Osnabrueck was one of the IRA's least successful in its fight to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Only one of three mortars fired at the barracks exploded and even that fell several yards (metres) short of its intended target, a diesel pump for military vehicles. No one was injured.
British forces in Germany have been a prime IRA target since the guerrilla group set off a car bomb at a British base near Moenchengladbach in 1987, injuring 31 people -- its first attack in Germany.
German and British anti-terrorist police have since worked together closely and Britain's Special Branch has a five-strong unit based in Cologne.

The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February. It has since set off a series of bombs in Britain, as well as the attack at Osnabrueck and a car bombing at the British army's headquarters in Northern Ireland in which one soldier was killed.
